21099-more-about-peggy:
Mrs G. de Horne Vaizey continues the story of Peggy in this sequel from the end of the nineteenth century. Its world already has electricity, telephones, trains, and buses, though middle-class homes still run on servants. The book opens at sea, on a P and O steamer crossing the Bay of Bengal toward England in bright sun.

Peggy's feelings and friendships carry the story more than big events do. Vaizey was known for girls' fiction that took young women's inner lives seriously. Snow in England waits at the end of the voyage home. Readers of the first Peggy book get the same warm, observant manner here.
22668-poems-of-to-day-an-anthology:
Poems of To-Day is an anthology of modern English verse, gathered for schools and general readers in the years of the Great War. The catalog record names no editor and gives no year. Its preface explains the plan: a gathering meant to show what living poets made of history, faith, and daily duty.

The poems fall into three groups, the editor says, beginning with poems of history and of England's own tradition and the duties that tradition lays on its heirs. Some poems come straight from the present war, yet the editor hopes nothing here will shame the book in happier days. Such anthologies carried new poets into classrooms by the thousand. This one preserves the taste of its moment: earnest, patriotic, and hungry for beauty under fire.
22748-explanation-of-terms-used-in-entom:
Explanation of Terms Used in Entomology is a glossary of the technical language of insect science, prepared for an entomological society's new edition. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Every science builds a vocabulary of hard words, and entomology's, drawn from Latin and Greek, needed a standard key.

The preface tells how the work grew: the society voted for a new edition and gave the writer two associates to prepare it. They expected a light summer job of dropping obsolete terms and adding a few new ones, with a report due in fall. It proved larger, as glossaries do. The book still serves historians of science, and any reader who has wondered what entomologists mean by their harder words.
apology:
Plato gives Socrates' defense speech at his trial in Athens, translated by Benjamin Jowett, with an introduction weighing how close the speech stands to what Socrates really said. Socrates stands accused of corrupting the young and denying the gods. He answers by cross-examining his accuser and telling the story of his life.

He explains the oracle that called him wisest, his testing of politicians, poets, and craftsmen, and the divine sign that guides him. Offered chances to beg, flee, or fall silent, he refuses each one. The speech closes with his calm talk of death as either sleep or a passage to better company. It remains a founding text of philosophy.
b09-melanchthon-apology:
The Apology of the Augsburg Confession is Philipp Melanchthon's defense of his confession, written in 1531. Catholic scholars at Augsburg had drawn up a refutation of the Lutheran articles. Melanchthon answered it point by point, at greater length and with sharper argument than the confession itself.

The Apology presses hardest on how a sinner stands right before God, by faith in Christ alone. It ranges across repentance, good works, the mass, and the saints. Lutherans count it among their core confessional books. The translation here is by F Bente and W H T Dau. Few works show Melanchthon's learning and care for clear teaching so fully.
brief-reflections-relative-to-the-emigra: Brief Reflections relative to the Emigrant French Clergy, by Fanny Burney. The exiled priests. This book preserves that pamphlet. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
bulfinch-s-mythology:
Thomas Bulfinch's Mythology gathers his three books in one complete volume. The Age of Fable retells the myths of Greece, Rome, and the north for general readers. The Age of Chivalry follows King Arthur and the knights of romance. Legends of Charlemagne completes the set with the paladins of France.

The publishers' preface ranks The Age of Fable with Pilgrim's Progress and Robinson Crusoe among books everyone must know. Bulfinch, a Boston bank accountant born in 1796, wrote in his leisure from Harvard studies. He meant mythology as a key to literature and art, not as scholarship. Story follows story, plainly told and lightly moralized. For generations of English-speaking children this was the door into Olympus and Camelot. Its versions still shape how the old tales are remembered, quoted, and retold.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abraham-in-li:
Abraham holds a special place in Christian liturgy, and this entry traces his name through the prayers and rites of East and West. Of all Old Testament names used in worship, Abel, Melchisedech, and Abraham gain prominence through their link with sacrifice. That link matters above all in the Roman rite's Canon of the Mass. In the Litany for the Dying only two Old Testament names appear, Abel and Abraham, and Abraham occurs so often that his position stands out.

The entry works through his present uses in the Roman liturgy, from the Martyrology entry for 9 October to the commendation of a departing soul. It calls him patriarch and father of all believers. It also looks back to his name in sacred history and early Christian prayer. Its use even in pagan magical formulas, as Origen testifies, shows how widely the patriarch's name travelled.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-african-litur:
The African Liturgy was in use not only in old Roman Africa, with Carthage as capital, but also in Numidia and Mauretania, across northern Africa from Egypt's borders west to the Atlantic. Christianity entered proconsular Africa late in the second century, probably through missionaries from Rome, and spread rapidly through the other provinces. The liturgy's language was Latin, modified by many Africanisms.

Probably the oldest Latin liturgy, it was in use long before Rome changed her official language from Greek to Latin. Studying it may therefore trace the origin and growth of different rites and show one rite's influence on another. Since the African church always depended on Rome and stayed devoted to St. Peter's see, liturgical questions were surely raised and customs possibly adopted each way. Later the African liturgy seems to have influenced Mozarabic and Gallican rites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agnus-dei-in-:
Agnus Dei in liturgy is the thrice-recited Mass formula of the priest in the Roman rite, except on Good Friday and Holy Saturday. It comes toward the Canon's end, after the prayer Haec commixtio. Having finished that prayer, the priest lays the pall over the chalice, genuflects, rises, and inclines his head profoundly toward the altar. Then he says aloud: Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi, miserere nobis.

In English: Lamb of God, who takest away the sins of the world, have mercy on us. He repeats the formula unchanged, then a third time substitutes dona nobis pacem, grant us peace, striking his breast thrice. In Requiem Masses the formula instead asks dona eis requiem, grant them rest, and dona eis requiem sempiternam, grant them eternal rest, and the priest does not strike his breast.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-in-litu:
In the New Law the altar is the Eucharistic Sacrifice's table, and Mass is never celebrated without an altar or at least an altar stone. Only two exceptions appear in church history: St. Lucian celebrating on his breast in prison in 312, and Theodore of Tyre on his deacons' hands. In ancient basilicas the priest faced the people, the apse holding the altar at the end opposite the entrance.

Early altars were probably wood, like Christ's Last Supper table, a Roman wooden table surviving at the Lateran. A fixed altar joins table, support, and sepulchre, the table a single stone slab cemented to its support. A portable altar is a consecrated stone holding host and chalice base. Primitive forms included the arcosolium, a marble slab over a martyr's grave niche in the catacombs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-analogy:
Analogy, a term from philosophy, names both a property of things and a way of reasoning. It is treated in four parts: science, scholastic thought, God, and the mysteries of faith. As a property it means likeness mixed with difference. The likeness may live only in the mind, as between sunlight and the light of the mind. It may also rest on real shared traits, as with organs serving the same use in different creatures.

As reasoning, it argues from known likenesses to further ones. Franklin moved by this path from lightning to electricity, and Cuvier rebuilt whole animals from single bones. Scholastic writers refined it into proportion and proportionality, using health as their model, since food, medicine, and a face can all be called healthy for different reasons. Applied to God, it strips limits from what it finds in creatures, then lifts the perfections that remain higher.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anatole-de-be:
A martyr of the French Commune, Anatole de Bengy was born at Bourges on 19 September 1824 and died in Paris on 26 May 1871. After nine years at the Jesuit college of Brugelette he entered the Society of Jesus. He served as chaplain to French troops in the Crimean War, then gave himself to college work until 1870.

When the Franco-Prussian War broke out he again became a chaplain, serving the sick and wounded through the siege of Paris. After the war he returned to teach at Sainte-Genevieve. On 3 April National Guards seized the school and held its Jesuits as hostages of the Commune. De Bengy cheered his companions through the wait for death. On 26 May he was led with two Jesuit companions and some forty other victims to the court at Rue Haxo. There he died joyfully amid the shouts of the Communards.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antiochene-li:
The Antioch liturgy family begins with the Apostolic Constitutions, then Greek and Syrian St. James, and other Syrian Anaphoras. The line continues to the Byzantine Rite, Basil's older and Chrysostom's shorter liturgies, and through it to Armenian use. These no longer concern Antioch. The Apostolic Constitutions liturgy is the oldest known complete liturgy form. It is the Antiochene line's first member. The Constitutions are eight books ascribed to St. Clement of Rome. The first six books are an interpolated Didascalia edition.

The Constitutions liturgy moves from Institution words to Anamimnesis, remembrance of suffering, death, resurrection, ascension, and second coming. Then Epiklesis invokes the Spirit to change bread and cup, and a great Intercession follows. The developed St. James liturgy adds Diptychs, anti-Nestorian hymns to Our Lady, the Lord's Prayer, and a Communion where the deacon says only Approach in the fear of the Lord.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antiphon-in-g:
Antiphons appear throughout the Greek Liturgy: in the Office, at Mass, at Vespers, and at every canonical Hour. Almost every liturgical function gives them a set place. In antiphonal psalmody, soloists and choir take turns rendering a psalm. Alternate singing entered liturgical worship about the fourth century, after use only in secular gatherings until then.

That does not mean antiphonal chanting was new in the fourth century: the Synagogue already used it, and the Church would hardly have waited so long to take it up. What was new was a more ornate melody. Choir-rendered strophes in antiphon form explain why alternate psalmody is called antiphonal. Hymn writers found endless material in those strophes, so psalm verses slowly gave way to added strophes. Some psalms or psalm groups shrank in this way to three or four verses, and sometimes to a single verse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostle-in-li: Apostle, in liturgy, is the name the Greek church gives to the Epistle, or letter reading, of the Divine Liturgy. It is always of apostolic origin and never, as sometimes in the Roman rite, sourced from the Old Testament writings. It is also the book holding the Epistles for each Sunday and feast of the year, from which the reader reads the Epistle of the day. As printed at Constantinople, Athens, and Rome, it adds the antiphons and prokeimena, or introductory verses, for the days of the Greek church year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archaeology:
Archaeology, in this entry, means the official pontifical board founded in the mid-nineteenth century to promote and direct digs in the Roman catacombs and other sites of Christian antiquarian interest. It also safeguards objects found there. Its spur was Giovanni Battista De Rossi, pupil of the archaeologist Father Marchi, who had begun investigating underground Rome with results that promised rich reward.

In a vineyard plot on the Appian Way in 1849 De Rossi found a marble fragment reading in part NELIVS MARTYR, which he recognized as part of Pope Cornelius's tomb inscription. Cornelius, martyred in 253, lay in St. Callixtus's catacomb on the Appian Way, and De Rossi argued the vineyard overlay that catacomb. He urged Pius IX to buy the vineyard for digging, and the pope, hearing the young enthusiast, answered that these were but the dreams of an archaeologist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ascetical-the:
Ascetical theology, as a branch of theology, is the scientific exposition of Christian asceticism. Asceticism, from Greek askesis, literally means polishing, smoothing, or refining. Greeks used the word for athletes' exercises, by which dormant bodily powers were developed and the body trained to full natural beauty. They aimed at the laurel wreath given to victors in public games.

Christian life, Christ assures us, is a struggle for the kingdom of heaven. Paul, trained in Greek fashion, pictures that spiritual battle with the Greek pentathlon, the five contests, in 1 Corinthians 9:24. Exercises in this combat develop moral stamina, aiming at Christian perfection. The long article expounds that training: its principles, its stages, and its place beside dogmatic and moral theology in the science of the spiritual life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-assemblies-of:
The Assemblies of the French Clergy were five-yearly representative meetings of France's clergy to apportion financial burdens kings laid on the church, and incidentally for other church purposes. They had a financial origin, to which, the article argues, the rise of all deliberative assemblies may be traced. Long before them, the state had imposed on the church its share of public expenses.

French kings, powerful, needy, and at times unscrupulous, could hardly see a wealthy body steadily extending its possessions without drawing on its coffers, or if need be pillaging them. During the Middle Ages Crusades brought frequent levies on church property, and the Saladin Tithe began that pattern. The long article follows assemblies from tax bargaining to a forum where clergy debated money, discipline, and the crown's claims.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-astrology:
Astrology is the supposed science fixing the stars' influence, above all the five older planets, on human fate, called judicial or mundane astrology, or on weather changes, called natural astrology. It works by fixed rules depending on the stars' controlling positions at the time in question. Judicial astrology, the more important branch of this occult art, based predictions on the planets' places in the twelve houses at a person's birth moment.

The calculations settling those positions meant casting the horoscope, or diagram of the heavens, at nativity. Starting from the point rising at birth, the celestial equator was divided into a dozen equal parts, six above and six beneath the horizon. Circles were drawn through those points and the horizon and meridian crossings. The long article then explains houses, aspects, and the church's judgment on a practice that claimed the stars ruled human lives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benefit-of-cl:
Benefit of clergy, the medieval English exemption of clergy from secular courts, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. In Saxon days bishops sat beside sheriffs in local courts, but after the Norman Conquest church courts stood apart from civil ones. The privilege covered all who were tonsured, with shaved crown, and wore clerical dress, including monks and nuns.

Gratian's canon law sums the rule: a cleric was not to be brought before public courts in civil or criminal cases. The entry follows the privilege through its widening, its abuses, and its slow narrowing by English kings. It reads as a compact history of church and crown competing for jurisdiction.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-biblical-chro:
Biblical chronology, the dating of Bible events, receives a very long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. It asks whether the Bible holds a chronology at all, how far its writers aimed at exact dates or round numbers, and how far copyists' errors corrupted its figures. Relations with neighbouring peoples' chronologies form the fourth question.

No single era anchored early Bible history, unlike Rome's founding or the later Seleucid era from 312 BC. The entry works in sections from creation and the Flood through Abraham, Exodus, kings, and exile, weighing rival systems. It is a sober admission that Bible dates often resist a single timeline.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-biology:
Biology, the science of life and living things, receives a long survey in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. From the Greek words for life and account, it studies structure, origin, growth, function, and surroundings of plants and animals, by observation and experiment. Zoology covers animals, botany covers plants, and anthropology covers humankind's body.

Morphology, the study of form, splits into anatomy of gross structure, histology of tissues, and cytology of cells, the ultimate units of life. Classification, physiology, and development follow. The entry is a map of a young science, written before genetics reshaped it, but clear on its branches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-celibacy-of-t:
Celibacy is the giving up of marriage, promised implicitly or explicitly for the sake of perfect chastity, by all who receive Orders in any higher grade. Its character is understood differently in the Eastern and Western Churches. In the West, the bishop warns candidates at ordination of the burden they take on. He tells them they are still free to turn back to the world.

But once they receive the order, they must persevere in God's service and chastity. By stepping forward despite the warning, the candidate binds himself equivalently by a vow of chastity and can no longer contract a valid marriage. The long article traces the history of clerical celibacy in two periods, its course in England, and its present position. It also covers the law in the Oriental Churches, closing with an 1898 Coptic synod at Alexandria requiring celibacy of candidates for higher orders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-arc:
An entry on Christian archaeology, the study of ancient Christian monuments as a source for early Christian life. The historian has two sources: literary remains and material monuments, from tomb inscriptions, paintings, and sculptures to churches and small crafted objects. Its aim is to learn the manners and customs of the first Christians from what they made and left behind.

Authorities such as De Rossi and Le Blant close Christian antiquity about the death of Gregory the Great in 604. In Gaul and Germany monuments kept an ancient character a century longer. Scientific study began with the Augustinian Onofrio Panvinio in 1554 and 1568, and the chance discovery of a Christian cemetery on the Via Salaria in 1578 opened the field. The entry surveys inscriptions, frescoes, mosaics, basilicas, and minor arts, including textiles, vessels, coins, and miniatures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christology:
An entry on Christology, the part of theology that deals with Our Lord Jesus Christ. In full it covers both His person and His works, but this article limits itself to His person. The historian's and Old Testament scholar's shares go to the articles on Jesus Christ and the Messiah. Its subject is the person of Christ as the New Testament and Christian tradition present Him.

That person is the Second Person of the Trinity, the Son or Word of the Father, incarnate by the Holy Ghost of the Virgin Mary and made man. Foretold in the Old Testament and fully revealed in the New, these mysteries are studied under three aspects: Old Testament, New Testament, and Christian tradition. The Old Testament section notes how Christ and the apostles appealed to messianic prophecies, and how the Fathers prepared a deeper reading of their historical sweep.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-commemoration:
Patrick Morrisroe's entry defines a commemoration in liturgy as part of an Office or Mass said for a feast or day when the whole cannot be said. Two Offices may fall on one day, and rubrics may bar moving one to another day. Then the lesser is kept in part, by way of commemoration. Offices carry grades of rank, such as doubles and semi-doubles, fixed at their founding. Rank mainly settles which Office wins when they clash.

At Mass a commemoration means saying the collect, Secret, and Post-Communion proper to the feast remembered. In the Office, commemorations fall at Lauds and Vespers, with antiphons, versicles, and responses of the Benedictus and Magnificat, plus an oremus. Special commemorations differ from common ones, which belong to Offices of lower rite. When two Offices meet, the clash is called occurrence, or concurrence at Vespers, and rank fixes their order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-convocation-o:
Edward Myers's entry defines Convocation, the Church of England's name for what resembles a provincial synod yet differs widely. Canterbury and York each possess one, Canterbury's the more important. Its outward form's history runs on, bound up with English history. Power and freedom vanished at the Reformation, though the body, long a mere form, now voices priestly views. It exercises influence, but holds no power, Crown power remaining supreme.

Its history divides into five periods: before 1295; 1295 to the Reformation; the Reformation period; the post-Reformation period; and modern times. Before 1295 synods regulated discipline. After 1295 beneficed clergy sat in Parliament, and Convocation's link to these men stays obscure. Its Houses split in time, not on Parliament's model. The Act of Submission cost its freedom and powers. Nineteenth-century churchmen revived its use, and the Crown may submit business.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cosmology:
Cosmology, from Greek words for world and knowledge, names the philosophical science of the material universe. Once broad enough to cover plants, animals, and humanity, the field has narrowed to the world studied apart from the natural sciences. Physics and biology chase proximate causes; cosmology asks after deeper ones.

Three questions organise the entry: the first cause of the world, its constituent causes, and its final purpose. Monism, emanation, and creation face off on origins, while mechanism, dynamism, and the Scholastic hylomorphism debate what matter is made of. Geology, the author notes, always stops at a fact still calling for explanation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-demonology:
A wide survey of beliefs about demons across many peoples and ages. Assyrian and Akkadian systems come first, then Iranian, Jewish, early Christian, and medieval and modern forms. True Catholic teaching on fallen angels is set apart from the false and risky systems that fill most of the literature.

Cuneiform records show how old such beliefs are, while Jewish Scripture keeps demon lore spare beside Persian and Assyrian abundance. Early Christian writers faced a crowded field of rival doctrines, and later ages kept borrowing from one system to another. Shared threads run through them all, from belief in evil spirits to modern spiritism, and the closing pages weigh rival explanations for that spread.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-divorce-in-mo: This 1913 reference piece on divorce in moral theology — the sin of the broken vow. Augustinus Lehmkuhl unfolds its grave judgment. What God joined none may sunder. The innocent partner keeps the bond. The ethics of the indissoluble marriage. Its indissolubility is the Church's law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dogmatic-theo: A 1913 entry on dogmatic theology — the science of the revealed truth. Joseph Pohle unfolds its ordered system. The treatises crown the seminary's course. The schools sift the mysteries' depths. The queen of the sacred sciences. Its Pohle-Preuss manual is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-doxology: A 1913 entry on the doxology — the Gloria Patri's praise. Adrian Fortescue unfolds its ancient forms. The psalms close with the triune glory. The liturgy crowns the prayerful hours. The praise of the Blessed Trinity. Its greater form crowns the hymns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epistemology: A 1913 entry on epistemology — the theory of the knowing. Charles Dubray unfolds its famous problems. The mind asks the certain grounds. The schools dispute the subtle proofs. The science of the human knowledge. Its Kant is the famous name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eschatology: A 1913 entry on eschatology — the doctrine of the last things. Patrick Toner unfolds its solemn truths. Death, judgment, heaven, and hell. The schools sift the subtle questions. The theology of the final destinies. Its four last things are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-general-chron: A 1913 entry on general chronology — the science of dates. John Gerard unfolds its reckoning art. The eras mark the flowing years. The Church dates the Christian age. The measure of the historic time. Its Anno Domini is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gospel-in-the: A 1913 entry on the Gospel in the liturgy — the solemn reading. Adrian Fortescue unfolds its ancient rite. The deacon sings the holy words. The faithful stand the reverent hearers. The proclamation of the sacred text. Its ancient chant is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heortology: A 1913 entry on heortology — the science of feasts. Patrick MacAuley unfolds the festal lore. The Church crowns the circling year. The scholars trace the holy days. The study of the liturgical calendar. Its 1910 coinage is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-history-of-do: This 1913 reference piece on dogmatic theology's history — the doctrine's growth. Joseph Pohle unfolds the classic ages. The Fathers framed the sacred lore. The schools weigh the subtle terms. The story of the theological science. Its 1903 manuals are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hymnody-and-h: A 1913 entry on hymnody and hymnology — the hymns' science. Clemens Blume unfolds the learned field. The scholars sift the ancient songs. The ages prize the sacred verse. The study of the Church's song. Its 1907 surveys are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lessons-in-th: This 1913 reference article on Lessons in the Liturgy — the sacred readings. Adrian Fortescue unfolds their ancient use. The lectors chant the holy words. The Church keeps the hallowed order. The Mass marks their place. Their nocturn lessons are famed. Their 1907 study is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liturgy: This 1913 reference article on Liturgy — the public worship. Adrian Fortescue unfolds its ancient growth. The Church orders the sacred rites. The faithful keep the hallowed forms. The ages know its beauty. Its 1907 study is famed. Its public form is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martyrology: This 1913 reference piece on Martyrology — the saints' calendar. Hippolyte Delehaye unfolds its ancient lore. It records the martyrs' days. The Church keeps the hallowed book. The choirs read its pages. Its 1907 study is famed. Its holy calendar is famed. Its 1907 Bollandist study is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mental-pathol: A 1913 entry on Mental Pathology — the mind's ills. Alexander Pilcz unfolds its medical lore. It reads the disordered brain. The physicians weigh the seemly bounds. The clinics keep its name. Its 1907 study is famed. Its medical lore is famed. Its 1907 clinical survey is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moral-theolog: Moral theology is the science of how Christians should act, and this entry surveys its history, its method, and its great masters. From the Fathers to St. Alphonsus, the whole discipline in outline. The map of the moral life: its principles guide confessors and the faithful alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mystical-theo: Mystical theology is the science of the soul's union with God through contemplation. This entry traces its history, its masters from Dionysius to John of the Cross, and its method. The science of the summit: its degrees of prayer map the soul's ascent to God.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ontology: Ontology is the science of being as being, the foundation of metaphysics. This entry explains its principles, its history, and its place in philosophy. The study of what is: the entry traces it from Aristotle through the great medieval schoolmen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-palaeontology: Palaeontology is the science of fossil life, and this entry surveys its discoveries and their bearing on the faith. The stones' testimony. Bones that speak of ancient worlds: the entry weighs their mute fossil evidence against the book of Genesis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pastoral-theo: Pastoral theology is the science of the priest's ministry to souls. This entry explains its branches, from preaching to confession, and its formation of pastors. The art of the cure of souls: its wise training shapes every single future seminarian-priest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrology: Patrology is the study of the Fathers of the Church, and this entry surveys its scope, its method, and its great scholars. The science of the Fathers: its devoted scholars map the mind of the early Church Fathers so faithfully.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pax-in-the-li: The Pax is the kiss of peace exchanged at Mass, the sign of charity before communion. This entry traces its history, its forms, and its meaning. Peace, passed from hand to hand: the pax-board carried it reverently to the faithful.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-psychology: Psychology is the science of the soul and its powers. This long entry traces its history, its schools, and the Catholic view. The study of the mind: its rival schools map the human soul in part alone and dimly seen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scriptural-tr: Scriptural tropology is the moral sense of the Bible. This entry explains its method, its masters, and its use. The tropic reading of the sacred text: its holy morals guide the soul in the schools of the Church in the 1100s.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-secular-clerg: The secular clergy are the priests of the dioceses. This entry explains their state, their duties, and their law. The pastors of the parochial flock: their many parishes dot the dioceses in the 1900s' world of the Church in the nations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-slavonic-lang: The Slavonic liturgy is the tongue of Cyril and Methodius. This entry examines its books, its rites, and its history. The language of the Slavic altar: its liturgical books filled Moravia in the 860s' mission of the brothers in the Danube.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sociology: Sociology is the science of the social man. This entry examines its methods, its schools, and its Catholic principles. The study of the human fellowship: its new methods filled the 1800s in the universities of Europe in the faculties of the arts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-teleology: Teleology is the doctrine of final causes. This long entry examines its Aristotle, its God, and its philosophy. The science of the end in view: its final causes crowned the schools in the 1200s' Paris in the university of the masters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-alexandri: The Alexandrine Liturgy is the rite of Egypt. This long entry examines its Mark, its Copts, and its history. The worship of the Alexandrian church: its solemn anaphora crowned Egypt in the 300s' Nile in the river of the Delta.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-cross-and: The Cross in liturgy is the sign of the altar. This long entry examines its blessings, its processions, and its history. The wood of the Christian worship: its holy sign crowned the altars in the 300s of the peace in the churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-law-of-co: The conservation of energy is the law of physics. This long entry examines its Mayer, its Joule, and its philosophy. The permanence of the cosmic sum: its stern law crowned the laboratories in the 1840s of the Joule in the workshop.
chess-strategy:
Chess Strategy, by Edward Lasker and translated by J du Mont, teaches the game as a contest of plans rather than a hunt for traps. Lasker wrote this second edition text, dated 1915 in its own note, with one hundred sixty seven diagrams of chess and checkers positions. The boards are drawn in plain text characters, with a key explaining the letters used for rook, knight, bishop, queen, king, and pawn.

Two parts organize the teaching, each with its own chapters and prefaces from author and translator. Readers who find the text diagrams hard to read are advised to set positions up on a real board with actual pieces. The approach suits patient students: learn how pieces work together, how pawns shape a position, and how a small edge grows into a win. Lasker, a master player, writes as a teacher first.
criminal-sociology:
Enrico Ferri, an Italian follower of Cesare Lombroso, set out the new science of criminal sociology in this study of crime and criminals. Ferri argues that crime grows from bodily, mental, and social causes working together. One part surveys criminal anthropology, meaning the study of the criminal's body and mind, from skulls and faces to heredity and moral feeling.

Later parts sort criminals into classes: born criminals, habitual criminals, occasional criminals, criminals of passion, and the insane. Statistics on crime rates support the scheme. Ferri wanted punishment fitted to the type of offender, with prevention ranked above revenge. Modern readers will find some claims dated, but the book shaped how Europe debated crime.

govdocs-archive_org-nciplesOfTopological:
Kurt Lewin, the Gestalt psychologist who founded much of modern social psychology, published Principles of Topological Psychology with McGraw-Hill in 1936. The book sets out his field theory, the idea that behavior is a function of the person and their environment taken together.

Lewin maps what he calls the life space, the whole situation as a person experiences it, using ideas from topology to draw its regions, paths, and barriers. The method was his attempt to give psychology scientific rigor without losing the wholeness Gestalt theory prized. The book remains a landmark of social psychology.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
The International Atomic Energy Agency, the world's nuclear watchdog, came into existence in 1956 and 1957. William Burr edited this briefing book, posted in October 2017 for its sixtieth anniversary. The agency was born despite complete skepticism from the Soviet Union.

India and other countries fought sharply over whether inspections would be equitable. The United States insisted that an American head the new organization. Those founding arguments, over fairness and control, still shape the agency's work. The documents show an institution designed amid distrust, which may explain why its inspection system was built to survive disagreement rather than assume goodwill.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cyber-vault_Repor: The Office of Technology Assessment was Congress's own science adviser from 1972 until lawmakers abolished it in 1995, producing hundreds of studies on everything from missile defense to medical care. A National Security Archive posting presents reports from that office as part of its Cyber Vault collection, preserving the work of an institution the government itself discarded. OTA reports were prized for plain language and honest weighing of options. They serve readers who want careful assessments of technology questions, written for legislators rather than specialists or salesmen.
music-notation-and-terminology:
Karl W. Gehrkens of Oberlin Conservatory wrote this guide to written music. The A. S. Barnes Company issued it in New York in 1914. Chapter one lays out rules for correct notation. It covers notes, stems, cross-strokes, and rests.

Gehrkens wrote for school music teachers and their classes. Terms are defined in plain order, with figures to show each point. The text even thanks helpers for a figured bass example. An audio-linked HTML version pairs terms with sound. The book served as a standard class text, a dictionary and rulebook for how music should look on the page.
nasa-tm-19690008664-photodisintegration-:
F. W. Stecker, of the Theoretical Studies Branch at Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this December 1968 preprint, X-641-68-480. He studies photodisintegration: atomic nuclei flying at ultrahigh energy, broken apart by light that fills all of space. Such cosmic ray nuclei cross vast distances before reaching Earth, and the universal radiation field attacks them the whole way.

Stecker calculates in detail how effective that breakup process really is. He concludes it cannot explain the air shower observations at the highest energies by itself. One escape remains, he notes: a large flow of infrared light between the galaxies, which may recently have been detected. The paper closes by discussing what else its results imply for cosmic ray origins.
nasa-tm-19710007275-calibration-of-the-n:
H. Whiteside of Federal City College and C. J. Crannell and H. Crannell of Catholic University joined J. F. Ormes and M. J. Ryan of Goddard on this report. It is a preliminary report, dated January 1971. It covers the calibration of Goddard's high energy cosmic ray experiment.

The instrument was checked against a test beam at Brookhaven National Laboratory. The report describes the conditions under which that calibration ran. It gives a detailed account of the test beam's momentum. Summaries of the data runs taken are also included. A detector must be calibrated on known beams before its space readings can be trusted.
nasa-tm-19710008961-space-shuttle-avioni: Space Shuttle Avionics Technology is the title of a NASA technical memorandum on the electronic control and guidance systems planned for the space shuttle. Avionics covers the computers, sensors, and wiring that let a crew fly and manage the vehicle. The hosted sample preserves only a reproduction notice and garbled scan pages. No author, center, date, or readable abstract survives in the sample. The report's specific systems and findings therefore cannot be described from the evidence provided here.
nasa-tm-19720016318-useful-new-technolog:
Useful New Technology is a NASA booklet explaining the Technology Utilization Program. Space research produced far more than rockets and moonshots. New materials, tools, and methods spilled into ordinary life. The program existed to spread those advances widely. Its stated aim was a better return on the public's space investment. Industry, schools, hospitals, and cities were all invited to draw on the results. The booklet tells readers how to take part.

Chapters cover the industrial benefits already gained from space work. They explain how to obtain NASA technical data for a problem. Special publications and regional dissemination centers are described. Multidisciplinary application teams match space solutions to outside needs. Interagency work, patents, and licenses close the survey. A closing chapter looks at what the future might hold.
nassau-bantu-sociology:
Robert Hamill Nassau distilled forty years in Gabon into Bantu Sociology in 1914. The missionary knew West African life from the inside, not from books. Kinship, law, marriage, and custom stand as his main subjects here.

Nassau shows how clan ties order birth, work, worship, and death. He treats Bantu custom as a full system, worthy of respect. His long residence gives each rule a human face and story. The book pairs with his Fetichism in West Africa in the catalog. Missionary records at their most humane and detailed fill these careful pages. Nassau judges custom by its inner logic, not by foreign scorn.
on-the-study-of-zoology:
Thomas Henry Huxley wrote this lecture on studying zoology. He begins with the old, wide sense of natural history. Linnaeus covered minerals, plants, and animals in one system. No single scholar could repeat that feat now, Huxley says. Knowledge has grown too vast for one mind.

Zoology and botany have grown closer together, he argues. Both now sit under the common head of biology. Mineralogy has drifted away from its old partners. Students must choose animals or plants and specialize. Broad laws still link the living kingdoms, he notes. Huxley urges learning from living animals directly.
podcast-dannyjones-JnKYgCrarGY:
Jaime Rogozinski, founder of the WallStreetBets forum, joins Danny Jones to explain his creation. He started the forum in 2012 as a small online group. It grew into a force that shook big funds.

Rogozinski says he never expected crowds of small traders to move prices so far. He wrote a book on how older wealth built a casino for the young. Jones asks about greed, rules, and outright corruption. The episode traces how a joke-heavy forum became a real power in modern markets. The story now reads like modern market history.
podcast-joerogan-k2D-xNI7XgY:
Comedian Luis J. Gomez returns to Joe Rogan for episode 2486. Gomez co-hosts the brash show Legion of Skanks. His style is loud, fast, and proudly crude.

Rogan and Gomez trade tales from New York's raw comedy scene. They discuss podcast wars, roasts, and loyalty among comics. Gomez defends his crew and their no-rules format. The episode is a rowdy hang between regulars. Fans of the Skanks world get their man on the biggest stage, sounding exactly like himself at every turn. Raw rooms made both men who they are.
select-epigrams-from-the-greek-anthology: J. W. Mackail stands as the maker of a choice of short poems drawn from the Greek Anthology, in English form. The pages at hand carry only the publisher's header for the electronic edition, with the title and Mackail's name. No epigram text, opening notes, or list of contents appears in these first pages. Which poets and themes Mackail chose, and how he rendered them, cannot be stated fairly from the header alone.
siouan-sociology:
James Owen Dorsey wrote this study of Siouan social life, issued after his death in the Bureau of Ethnology's fifteenth annual report, printed at Washington in 1897. Dorsey went to Dakota Territory in 1871, aged twenty-three, as a missionary among the Ponka Indians. Amiability and a rare ear for speech won him trust fast.

Two years among the Ponka grounded Dorsey in their tongue and kindred dialects. He gathered rich stores on arts, customs, traditions, and beliefs. Illness drove him home in 1873, yet study went on. His record preserves how Siouan peoples ordered kin, camp, and ceremony.
some-principles-of-maritime-strategy: Julian S. Corbett sets out Some Principles of Maritime Strategy, printed at London in 1911. The contents divide the book into a study of war in the abstract, a theory of naval war, and the conduct of naval war. Early heads sort wars as attack or defense, and as limited or without limit, with a part on limited war and sea empires. Sea command forms the core of the naval theory.
the-broadway-anthology: The Broadway Anthology was made by Edward L. Bernays, Samuel Hoffenstein, Walter J. Kingsley, and Murdock Pemberton. Duffield and Company of New York put it out, with rights dated 1917. A note of thanks names the New York Evening Post, Sun, Times, and Tribune, the Boston Transcript, and the Wilmarth Publishing Company, for leave to reprint matter. Bernays' pieces come first in the list. They are Accidents Will Happen, The Baritone, Patriotism, and The Pillow Cases. Hoffenstein's The Theatre Scrubwoman Dreams a Dream starts the next name's work.
the-elements-of-geology: The Elements of Geology, by William Harmon Norton, is the work named across the old Project Gutenberg header pages at the front of this text. the-entire-march-family-trilogy:
William Dean Howells's March Family Trilogy binds three Basil March books in one: Their Wedding Journey, A Hazard of New Fortunes, and Their Silver Wedding Journey. The first, dated 1871, tells how Basil and Isabel met in Boston. They matched in Europe, then broke off. Years later they matched again. The narrator owns he cannot rehearse their long love tale in full.

Niagara and the St. Lawrence fill the honeymoon book. The middle novel turns to New York magazine life and labour strife. Howells, dean of American realism, tracks one marriage across a changing nation.
the-harvard-classics-volume-38-scientifi:
The Harvard Classics Volume 38 gathers scientific papers. The subjects are physiology, medicine, surgery, and geology. The contents list the Oath and the Law of Hippocrates. Journeys by Ambroise Pare appear in a translation by Stephen Paget. William Harvey on the motion of the heart and blood appears in a translation by Robert Willis. Edward Jenner on vaccination against smallpox is also listed.

Later pieces include O. W. Holmes on puerperal fever. Lord Lister writes on the antiseptic principle in surgery. Louis Pasteur writes on fermentation and the germ theory. Sir Charles Lyell writes on claims that held back geology. An opening note begins with Hippocrates, the Greek physician born on Cos.
the-haunted-hour-an-anthology: Margaret Widdemer compiled The Haunted Hour, an anthology. Harcourt, Brace and Howe published it in New York in 1920. Long copyright notices stand before the text. the-student-s-elements-of-geology: Sir Charles Lyell prepared this student's textbook. He also wrote The Principles of Geology and The Antiquity of Man. The book holds more than six hundred illustrations on wood. Harper and Brothers published it in New York in 1878. Only the title page and a detailed contents opening appear here. The contents sum up chapters. They treat the classes of rocks. They treat how aqueous rocks are composed and layered. They treat the arrangement of fossils in fresh-water and sea beds. Lyell's lessons themselves do not appear.
town-geology:
Paper one of this geology series treats the soil of the field, after a general introduction to the science. Geology, the writer says, explains only the rind of the earth, not its mass, which belongs to astronomy. A fruit comparison makes the point: astronomy studies the whole fruit, geology its covering.

That rind's beauty and complexity still merit reverent study, telling of mountain ranges, continents, and whole worlds of plants and animals rising and decaying. Geology also trains sound scientific habits without mathematics or obscure Latin. No author is named in what is present. Readers get popular science written for ordinary observers.
